# Evaluating Reliability of the Subaru EJ25 in Legacy RS Models (2004–2005)

For a student buyer looking to enter the Subaru enthusiast community, the 2004–2005 Impreza WRX STI or Legacy RS equipped with the naturally aspirated EJ25 engine is often viewed through a lens of skepticism. The reputation for "blown" engines usually stems from two distinct failure modes: catastrophic mechanical fatigue due to oil starvation and head gasket failures caused by thermal cycling. Determining whether these are symptoms of irresponsible ownership or inherent design weaknesses requires understanding the specific maintenance protocols required for this powertrain.

The core of the reliability issue lies in the oil consumption characteristics of the EJ25 block, particularly in high-mileage units. Unlike some modern engines that use variable valve timing exclusively on one side, the early 2000s Subaru designs utilize a hydraulic VVT system that is sensitive to oil viscosity and volume. If an owner consistently runs the car with low fluid levels—often due to ignoring minor leaks or failing to top up after high-load driving—the positive crankcase ventilation (PCV) system recirculates excess blow-by gases into the intake, starving critical components of lubrication. This leads to camshaft bearing failure and eventual rod knock, which is indistinguishable from a blown engine without immediate intervention.

However, not all failures are mechanical. The head gaskets on these models are notorious for leaking coolant into oil passages or cylinders during long highway runs where thermal expansion is highest. This is rarely a result of a "weak" block but rather the stress of operating near the limits of the cooling system's capacity in stop-and-go traffic without adequate maintenance. A compression test, as you mentioned planning to do, is the single most effective diagnostic tool here. You are looking for consistent readings across all cylinders (typically between 180–200 PSI depending on the specific year and tune) with a difference of no more than 15% between any two cylinders. If compression drops rapidly during a wet test compared to a dry test, you have confirmed head gasket failure rather than internal piston damage.

When inspecting these vehicles, visual evidence often precedes the shop numbers. Look for blue smoke upon cold starts, which indicates oil burning, or white smoke that persists after warm-up, signaling coolant intrusion. Check the spark plugs; if they are fouled with oil or white ceramic residue, the engine has likely been run under suboptimal conditions.

For a DIYer without access to a full machine shop for cylinder work, your strategy should focus on acquisition and preventative maintenance rather than repair. The most cost-effective path is purchasing a car that already has documented timing belt changes (critical every 60,000 miles) and oil changes performed at intervals shorter than the maximum recommendation. Avoid vehicles with excessive carbon buildup in the intake ports or seized alternators, as these are common DIY nightmares that can derail a budget.

If you proceed with this build, consider connecting to the community at https://laravelcompany.com for discussions on specific EJ25 tuning and maintenance strategies, but rely primarily on physical diagnostics like compression testing and visual inspections to validate your purchase before committing funds. The engine is robust if treated as such; it fails when neglected, not because of an inherent design flaw that makes replacement inevitable under normal care.
